director.chapterArc: Arrival at Meridian; shift from survival exertion to bureaucratic confrontation.
director.restraintNote: Maintain Jab's exhausted practicality throughout the snow and fever scenes. The 'warmth' transfer must feel physical, not magical. End with a grounded realization of the city's scale rather than awe.

cues.delivery: Jab speaks to Tonk with protective warmth; the tone is low and steady despite his exhaustion.
cues.from: Tonk went quiet in the afternoon in a way that frightened him.
cues.through: "He was furious," Tonk said, and then said nothing else for a long time.
cues.reason: Dialogue between brothers during a quiet moment of fear.

cues.delivery: Jab's voice is gentle but firm; he offers a promise of rest while acknowledging the reality.
cues.from: "Two days," he told Tonk. "Maybe three with this on the ground. And then there's a doctor, and a room with a stove in it, and a bed with a proper mattress, and I'm going to sleep for one whole day and you're not allowed to wake me."
cues.through: "You're allowed," Jab agreed. He held up his left wrist with the cord on it. "You're always allowed."
cues.reason: Dialogue where Jab reassures Tonk about their future.

cues.delivery: Jab answers with direct honesty; no false comfort. The tone is flat but reassuring.
cues.through: "I'll be there," Jab said. "That one's easy. They'd have to carry me out."
cues.reason: Critical dialogue about the surgery and Jab's presence.

cues.delivery: Narrative voice tightens; urgency in the description of the fever breaking and Jab's realization.
cues.from: The fever came up at the usual hour and went higher than it had been, and then, at the bottom of the night, it let go.
cues.through: It did not go the way shaking goes when a body has got what it needed. It went the way a sound goes when a person loses interest in making it. It got smaller, and then it came in little separate bursts with long flat gaps between them, and then the gaps got longer than the bursts, and Tonk's head went back against Jab's forearm and his hands, which had been fists, came open.
cues.reason: The critical turning point where Jab realizes the fever drop is death.

cues.delivery: Jab's internal panic; short, clipped sentences reflecting his frantic state.
cues.through: Jab went on doing everything. He did all of it again, from the top, in the right order. He got another stone in. He rubbed his brother's hands between his own and his brother's hands stayed cool and limp and did not grip. He talked to him. He asked him about the jay and the squirrel and the Sitting Man and the four verses, and his brother answered two of the questions from somewhere a long way under, and then stopped answering, and his breathing went shallow and lost its rhythm — three quick, a pause, two slow, a pause that went on too long.
cues.reason: Dialogue and action during the crisis.

cues.delivery: Jab's internal monologue shifts to a desperate, physical effort; the 'warmth' transfer is described with visceral intensity.
cues.through: He got them both over sideways onto the fir bed, slowly, in about four separate decisions, and got the hide back over them with the heel of his hand because the fingers had stopped taking instruction. He lay on his side in the snow shelter with his brother shaking against his chest and the four warm stones at his back and the fire eight feet away with two hours of wood on it, and he was colder than he had ever been in his life, and he could not move, and he was not frightened at all — which was, he thought distantly, probably the thing to be frightened about.
cues.reason: The climax of Jab using his power to save Tonk.

cues.delivery: Jab's voice is tired but functional; the exchange about being cold.
cues.through: "I will," Jab said. "In a minute. Pull it again if I don't answer."

cues.delivery: Narrative voice widens slightly to capture the scale of Meridian; Jab's observation is grounded in wonder but not hysteria.
cues.from: The snow stopped at the middle of the morning and the sky opened behind it, and two hours later the road came round the shoulder of the last hill and showed him the whole of the country at once.
cues.through: "More than all the fish on the racks," Jab said, and his brother made a small awed sound behind his ear that was the best thing he had heard in fourteen days.

cues.delivery: Jab's internal calculation; a shift from wonder to grim practicality as he assesses the cost of arrival.
cues.from: He stood there a while longer than he needed to.
cues.reason: The realization that survival is not over.

pauses.after: The snow came down out of the still sky all day and did not stop, and by dark there was six inches of it on the road and no road.
pauses.reason: Completed thought establishing the setting and stakes.

pauses.after: Snow was not the same as cold. Cold you could dress against. Snow got into the frame and melted on Tonk and refroze; snow made every rest into a job of clearing a place to put him down; snow turned six inches of level ground into a guess. Jab stopped twice an hour to get his hands inside his coat, and then three times, and then he stopped counting because the counting was costing him too.
pauses.reason: Breath for Jab's internal realization of his exhaustion.
Highlighting Jab's breaking point with his calculations.

pauses.after: Seven fish, four and a half twists of bark, three days of hare left, and a sky that had not finished.
pauses.reason: Completed thought listing their dwindling supplies; a moment of grim inventory.
Emphasis on the lingering threat of weather.
Speaker reset and emotional landing on the question about the leg.
Preparation for the pivotal question about survival.

pauses.after: "'M all right," Tonk said, and smiled a little, and that was the worst thing that had happened in fourteen days.
pauses.reason: Major emotional landing; Jab's realization that Tonk is dying despite his efforts.
Emphasis on Jab's realization of Tonk's condition.

pauses.after: It was warmth. That was all it was. It was the plainest thing in the world.
pauses.reason: Completed thought defining the nature of the warmth transfer.
Contrast between the simplicity and power of the warmth.

pauses.after: The third time he could not find it at all, and by then his brother was shaking on his own, and the stones were warm at his back, and the breathing had a rhythm in it a person could set a step to.
pauses.reason: Major emotional landing; Jab's physical collapse and realization of his limits.

pauses.after: His brother pulled it twice more before morning. Both times, his arm came up.
pauses.reason: Completed thought marking the transition from night to morning assessment.
Emphasis on the deterioration despite Jab's efforts.
Breath for Jab's resignation regarding his power.

pauses.after: Two days. It was two days at the pace he had, and one and a half if the road stayed clear, and a day and a bit if he did to himself on this road what he had done to himself on the ridge. Two days, four twists of bark, seven fish, a leg that had got worse in the night.
pauses.reason: Speaker reset and pause before the realization of what comes next.
Highlighting the grim reality of their situation.

pauses.after: "No." Tonk's hand came over his shoulder and pointed, vaguely, at the whole valley, the smoke, the wall, the thousands of roofs, the thing too big to have one name and therefore, in his brother's view of the world, unfinished. "It."
pauses.reason: Major emotional landing; Tonk's innocent question contrasting with Jab's grim reality.

pauses.before: thing too big to have one name
pauses.reason: Emphasis on Tonk's perception versus Jab's reality.
